demonstrations.review: I thought my first one was defective, but the 2nd one also doesn't work. Cannot easily remove case to install batteries - need some time of mini philips screwdriver. Had a DC plug which works, but the red guy either cannot inflate, or when he does he just stands straight up and doesn't move. Guess you get what you pay for when it's this cheap.

demonstrations.item_text:
Blue Book Guide to Preserving
Paperback – January 1, 2017

The ultimate guide for creating your own signature foods. Over 500 recipes. Canning, freezing, and cooking recipes featuring step-by-step recipe format and color photography. Nutritious meal creation recipes using home canned foods. Icons to find: tips on customizing flavors, ingredients, and recipe yield to fit individual family needs; helpful instructions on Canning techniques; ingredient Preparation; meal options; and more.
demonstrations.review: Really bummed out by this book. It gives a GREAT overview of canning, but each recipe requires I use Ball Brand spices or canning additives. They should give a pickling spice recipe I could make myself instead of relying on a prepackaged ball product. I ended up returning the book. Otherwise, I would've given this 5 stars.

target.item_text:
The Truth About Forever

From the award-winning and New York Times bestselling author of Once and for All Expect the unexpected. Macy’s got her whole summer carefully planned.   But her plans didn’t include a job at Wish Catering. And they certainly didn’t include Wes.   But Macy soon discovers that the things you expect least are sometimes the things you need most. “Dessen gracefully balances comedy with tragedy and introduces a complex heroine worth getting to know.” — Publishers Weekly Sarah Dessen is the winner of the Margaret A. Edwards Award for her contributions to YA literature, as well as the Romantic Times Career Achievement Award. Books by Sarah Dessen: That SummerSomeone Like YouKeeping the MoonDreamlandThis LullabyThe Truth About Forever Just ListenLock and KeyAlong for the RideWhat Happened to GoodbyeThe Moon and MoreSaint Anything Once and for All
target.review: Perhaps I should have heeded that caveat going in. As a teen, as someone else noted, I probably would have loved this. As an adult I found the characters pretty one dimensional and somtimes downright irritating. Having lost my own mom at 17, I felt like I should have connected with Macy on some level, but I didn't. The whole "I have to be perfect now to keep from ever getting hurt again" is so cliche and not at all the messy way emotions are handled in real life. Her 'boyfriend' Jason was text-book type-A and there was no reason at all she should have liked him to begin with. Then again, I didn't find Macy all that interesting either. Ultimately it the book was saved by its quick pace and likable side characters, even though to an extent even those "wacky" ones were overdrawn. I just can't bring myself to only give it two stars, because once I started the book, it was a very quick read. I read it because it was recommended by a blogger who highlights YA fiction that adults will like too...I just don't know what the big appeal is for this one.

demonstrations.item_text:
Sand: Omnibus Edition
Paperback – January 4, 2014

We live across the thousand dunes with grit in our teeth and sand in our homes. No one will come for us. No one will save us. This is our life, diving for remnants of the old world so that we may build what the wind destroys. No one is looking down on us. Those constellations in the night sky? Those are the backs of gods we see.
demonstrations.review: Ever since I read Wool, I've desperately wanted to love another book by Hugh Howey as much. And I never have, Sand being no exception. I forced myself to get to where I was and finally gave up in the middle. There are too many books to read for me to try to finish something I don't like. I wanted to hear more about the diving, and the reason everything was covered in sand to begin with. I wanted Palmer to explore the Sandscraper! Ultimately I found it too wordy, overly descriptive and boring.

demonstrations.item_text:
The Night Sister: A Novel
Kindle Edition

The latest novel from New York Times best-selling author Jennifer McMahon is an atmospheric, gripping, and suspenseful tale that probes the bond between sisters and the peril of keeping secrets. Once the thriving attraction of rural Vermont, the Tower Motel now stands in disrepair, alive only in the memories of Amy, Piper, and Piper's kid sister, Margot. The three played there as girls until the day that their games uncovered something dark and twisted in the motel's past, something that ruined their friendship forever.      Now adult, Piper and Margot have tried to forget what they found that fateful summer, but their lives are upended when Piper receives a panicked midnight call from Margot, with news of a horrific crime for which Amy stands accused. Suddenly, Margot and Piper are forced to relive the time that they found the suitcase that once belonged to Silvie Slater, the aunt that Amy claimed had run away to Hollywood to live out her dream of becoming Hitchcock's next blonde bombshell leading lady. As Margot and Piper investigate, a cleverly woven plot unfolds—revealing the story of Sylvie and Rose, two other sisters who lived at the motel during its 1950s heyday. Each believed the other to be something truly monstrous, but only one carries the secret that would haunt the generations to come.
demonstrations.review: I love Jennifer McMahon and her ability to be creepy without being downright scary (although I'd say that The Winter People is scarier). I prefer listening to books but I did read this one straight through, as it hit just the right note of creepiness and mystery. I give four stars simply due to one particular issue I had with what happened to Rose's sister, but don't want to post spoilers. It just seemed too convenient the way it wrapped up that particular part of the story.

demonstrations.item_text:
Summers at Castle Auburn
Library Binding – January 1, 2008

As a child, Coriel Halsing spent many glorious summers at Castle Auburn with her half-sister-and fell in love with a handsome prince who could never be hers. But now that she is a young woman, she begins to see the dark side of this magical place...
demonstrations.review: I love Sharon Shinn - she really has opened the door for me to fantasy romance, mostly because with her writing I'm not reading pages and pages of world building or about dragons or other nonsense. It's almost like reading historical romance with some magic thrown in. That said, Summers at Castle Auburn did not disappoint. While generally predictable (you can kind of easily figure out who will end up with whom) I thought it all came together very well. Particularly Corie's maturation (although it did seem like she needed a potion to speed this up?) and her realization that Bryan is not all he seems and that the aliora do not deserve their fate. I would have liked to have read more about the development of her relationship with Kent, as the ending seemed a little abrupt, but all in all, it was great.

demonstrations.item_text:
The Explorer's Code: A Novel
Hardcover – June 28, 2011

Award-winning CNN journalist Kitty Pilgrim turns her talents to print in The Explorer’s Code, an exciting international thriller that revolves around the quest for a land deed valuable enough to kill for. When the renowned young oceanographer Cordelia Stapleton receives an invitation to accept an award on behalf of her great-great-grandfather, a famous Victorian polar explorer, she has no idea her life is about to change dramatically. John Sinclair—a dashing, wealthy archaeologist and philanthropist—presents Cordelia with the award at the glamorous Oceanographic Institute Ball in Monaco. He also gives her a journal that her greatgreat- grandfather wrote in 1908. An orphan with very few family belongings, Cordelia is amazingly touched to have this precious heirloom. Once the journal is in her possession, Cordelia learns that she is heir to the land on which the Global Seed Vault in Norway sits. The valuable deed for this land, or at least a clue to its whereabouts, may be hidden in the journal. When the journal disappears from Cordelia’s stateroom on the Queen Victoria and Cordelia receives threatening e-mails, it becomes clear that she is in danger. John Sinclair comes to Cordelia’s aid, helping her search for the missing journal and land deed, and capturing her heart. As they race to find the deed, Cordelia and Sinclair encounter a team of British virologists trying to decode the genome of the 1918 influenza pandemic, but unearthing infected tissue samples may prove more lethal than curative. Cordelia and Sinclair sail through the Mediterranean from Monaco to an archaeological site in Ephesus, Turkey. They travel to a beautiful old Parisian home and a lavish estate in the British countryside. Their search culminates in the high Arctic archipelago of Svalbard, not far from the North Pole. Behind them every step of the way are a consortium of Russian underworld criminals, religious fanatics from Texas, a sinister botanist, and a sexy American spy, all hunting for the deed, all pursuing Cordelia. The Explorer’s Code is a satisfying blend of historical detail, fast-paced action, scientific discovery, and the thrill of exploration that informs as well as entertains. The breathtaking ending in the high Arctic is as chilling as a polar breeze.
demonstrations.review: This is the first review I've ever left, but I've been reading them for years. I was prompted when I realized that the other reviews I read for this book made it seem much better than it was. The plot is interesting, and the action moves quickly enough, but in my opinion it's ruined by the stilted and ubelievable dialogue. I swear, every sentence of dialogue starts with the name of whoever the speaker is addressing. It's as though the author thinks we might forget their names?? Hardly possible, since they're repeated approximately 4,000 times. The romance moves too quickly and is equally as unbelievable. All in all, even though the flu info and the lost deed plot were interesting and well-intertwined, it was too much to overcome. I didn't feel at all connected to any of the characters.

demonstrations.item_text:
I Let You Go
Hardcover – May 3, 2016

THE NEW YORK TIMES BESTSELLER One of The New York Times Book Review’ s 10 Best Crime Novels of 2016! The next blockbuster thriller for those who loved The Girl on the Train and Gone Girl. ..“a finely crafted novel with a killer twist.”( #1 New York Times bestselling author Paula Hawkins) On a rainy afternoon, a mother's life is shattered as her son slips from her grip and runs into the street... I Let You Go follows Jenna Gray as she moves to a ramshackle cottage on the remote Welsh coast, trying to escape the memory of the car accident that plays again and again in her mind and desperate to heal from the loss of her child and the rest of her painful past.    At the same time, the novel tracks the pair of Bristol police investigators trying to get to the bottom of this hit-and-run. As they chase down one hopeless lead after another, they find themselves as drawn to each other as they are to the frustrating, twist-filled case before them. Elizabeth Haynes, author of Into the Darkest Corner , says, “I read I Let You Go in two sittings; it made me cry (at least twice), made me gasp out loud (once), and above all made me wish I'd written it...a stellar achievement.”
demonstrations.review: I really liked the first part of the novel more than the 2nd. I liked it's slow pace and Jenna's characterization as she gets to know her new surroundings. The 2nd half felt like the author was trying a little too hard for a Gone Girl-esque vibe that didn't quite make it. Without any spoilers, I found the reasoning behind everything Jenna did to be very flawed. I suppose people are flawed, but this was a little too much to swallow. There were things that were also a little too neatly tied up and unresolved between Ray, Kate, Mags, and Tom, the son. So maybe there is going to be another novel w/ these detectives? That's what it felt like.

target.item_text:
The First Prophet (A Bishop Files Novel)
Paperback – November 27, 2012

A woman with extraordinary abilities is drawn into a shocking conspiracy in the first thriller in the Bishop Files series—from the New York Times bestselling author of the Bishop/SCU novels. Within the FBI, there exists a team of psychics whose powers cannot be denied. But these agents are feared—by a cabal of conspirators with only one weapon: to blind the psychics to the evils all around them. Months ago Sarah Gallagher woke from a coma with psychic abilities she couldn’t control. They changed her life and cost her the man she loved. And now, someone is playing games with Sarah’s mind. It begins with Sarah’s home being destroyed by fire—an act of arson that draws novelist Tucker Mackenzie into Sarah’s confidence. But he has other reasons for pursuing a woman who can see what others can’t. So does a mysterious enemy intent on eliminating Sarah, and everyone she cares about. Because it’s only a matter of time before her visions lead her and Tucker to a secret many will kill to hide...
target.review: Love most of Kay Hooper's stories but this one left me wanting. It's a starter for a new set of stories,so it just set's things up with no real conclusion. While I would like to read more about  the main characters this one was incomplete

demonstrations.item_text:
The Last Woman Standing: A Novel

At once an epic account of an improbable romance and a retelling of an iconic American tale, The Last Woman Standing recalls the famed gunfight at the O.K. Corral through the eyes of a spunky heroine who sought her happy ending in a lawless outpost—with a fierce will and an unflagging spirit. Two decades after the Civil War, Josephine Marcus, the teenage daughter of Jewish immigrants, is lured west with the promise of marriage to Johnny Behan, one of Arizona’s famous lawmen. She leaves her San Francisco home to join Behan in Tombstone, Arizona, a magnet for miners (and outlaws) attracted by the silver boom. Though united by the glint of metal, Tombstone is plagued by divided loyalties: between Confederates and Unionists, Lincoln Republicans and Democrats. But when the silver-tongued Behan proves unreliable, it is legendary frontiersman Wyatt Earp who emerges as Josephine’s match. As the couple’s romance sparks, Behan’s jealousy ignites a rivalry destined for the history books…
demonstrations.review: Interesting tale of Wyatt's love interest. It tells of how they met and Tombstone. I really feel that while it was a good read I'd like to see what happened after they got together in San Fran, so give me a sequel.

demonstrations.item_text:
Go, Dog. Go! (Beginner Books(R))
Kindle Edition

P.D. Eastman's canine classic—perfect for fans of the Netlix Original Go, Dog. Go! animated preschool series! Written for beginning readers using only 75 different words, this beloved Beginner Book by P.D. Eastman—edited by Dr. Seuss—features all kinds of wonderful dogs riding bicycles, scooters, skiis, roller skates, and driving all sorts of vehicles on their way to a party held on top of a tree! This is a perfect gift for P.D. Eastman fans and dog lovers of all ages! Originally created by Dr. Seuss himself, Beginner Books are fun, funny, and easy to read. These unjacketed hardcover early readers encourage children to read all on their own, using simple words and illustrations. Smaller than the classic large format Seuss picture books like The Lorax and Oh, The Places You'll Go!, these portable packages are perfect for practicing readers ages 3-7, and lucky parents too! "The canine cartoons make an elementary text funny and coherent and still one of the best around."-- School Library Journal.
demonstrations.review:
It's fun and teaches about opposites and color. Dogs are up , out, on ,in, over , under etc..
Also stop/go lights. My 2 year old granddaughter has the book but she likes it best when we read it on my Kindle Fire.

demonstrations.item_text:
Kipper's Kite: [Touch and Feel]
Board book – October 1, 2002

Kipper's new kite is perfect for flying--and for having a good time with his friends!
demonstrations.review: My 2 year old granddaughter loves the Kipper the Dog cartoons so I wanted to find a book for her. Since it is an old English show most  are out of print. I found a used one that is in great shape. She loves it, especially the "touch part" where she can feel different textures. Very cute

demonstrations.item_text:
Concealed in Death
Hardcover – February 18, 2014

Lieutenant Eve Dallas uncovers a conspiracy when she investigates the murders of some of New York City's troubled youth in this thriller in the #1 New York Times bestselling In Death series. Leading the demolition of a long-empty New York building that once housed a makeshift shelter for troubled teenagers, Lieutenant Eve Dallas’s husband uncovers two skeletons wrapped in plastic. And by the time Eve’s done with the crime scene, there are twelve murders to be solved.The victims are all young girls. A tattooed tough girl who dealt in illegal drugs. The runaway daughter of a pair of well-to-do doctors. They all had their stories. And they all lost their chance for a better life.Then Eve discovers a connection between the victims and someone she knows. And she grows even more determined to reveal the secrets of the place that was called The Sanctuary—and the evil concealed in one human heart.
demonstrations.review: This my favorite series, I have read all of the books several times. While the story is an okay mystery it's just not the same. I can only surmise that the author wrote an outline and then handed it off to someone else. The tell is the way these well known and loved characters interact, it's just not true to the other books. Something is missing, it's very disappointing and obvious that this is an imitation. I also noticed this edition is missing Nora's( J.D. Robb's) picture. Maybe she got tired of the series which is a shame because it is her best. I think I'll read the old ones to recapture the magic, I feel somehow cheated.

demonstrations.item_text:
Trick of the Light (Trickster, Book 1)
Mass Market Paperback – September 1, 2009

View our feature on Rob Thurman’s Trick of the Light . When Trixa learns of a powerful artifact known as the Light of Life, she knows she’s hit the jackpot. Both sides—angel and demon—would give anything for it. But first she has to find it. And as Heaven and Hell ready for an apocalyptic throwdown, Trixa must decide where her true loyalty lies, and what she’s ready to fight for. Because in her world, if you line up on the wrong side, you pay with more than your life…
demonstrations.review: There's a lot of urban fantasies out there but I have to say this one is right on top. It's full of action and twists. The main character is female and has Loki backing her up (not that she needs him). There's no mooning over vampires or werewolves, it's not for the Twilight crowd. Just got the next book The Grimrose Path, I'm halfway through and it's a keeper too.

target.item_text:
Gone Girl: A Novel
Kindle Edition

#1 NEW YORK TIMES BESTSELLER • The “mercilessly entertaining” ( Vanity Fair ) instant classic “about the nature of identity and the terrible secrets that can survive and thrive in even the most intimate relationships” (Lev Grossman, Time )—now featuring never-before-published deleted scenes NAMED ONE OF THE MOST INFLUENTIAL BOOKS OF THE DECADE BY CNN AND ONE OF THE BEST BOOKS OF THE DECADE BY TIME AND ENTERTAINMENT WEEKLY NAMED ONE OF THE TEN BEST BOOKS OF THE YEAR BY Janet Maslin, The New York Times • People • Entertainment Weekly • O: The Oprah Magazine • Slate • Kansas City Star • USA Today • Christian Science Monitor On a warm summer morning in North Carthage, Missouri, it is Nick and Amy Dunne’s fifth wedding anniversary. Presents are being wrapped and reservations are being made when Nick’s clever and beautiful wife disappears. Husband-of-the-Year Nick isn’t doing himself any favors with cringe-worthy daydreams about the slope and shape of his wife’s head, but passages from Amy's diary reveal the alpha-girl perfectionist could have put anyone dangerously on edge . Under mounting pressure from the police and the media—as well as Amy’s fiercely doting parents—the town golden boy parades an endless series of lies, deceits, and inappropriate behavior. Nick is oddly evasive, and he’s definitely bitter—but is he really a killer? NAMED ONE OF THE BEST BOOKS OF THE YEAR BY San Francisco Chronicle • St. Louis Post-Dispatch • The Chicago Tribune • HuffPost • Newsday
target.review: Really enjoyed this book, the development of the characters, the two main characters telling their "love" story.  Also, great plot twist.  I wasn't thrilled with the direction the author took at the end of the story and then it just-ended.  It was like she didn't know what else to write and hurried up and put anything.  I would give most of the book 5 stars but the end of the book brought it down to 3.

demonstrations.item_text:
A Criminal Defense (Philadelphia Legal)
Kindle Edition

Part 1 of the "Philadelphia Legal" Series Losing the trial of his life could mean losing everything.When a young reporter is found dead and a prominent Philadelphia businessman is accused of her murder, Mick McFarland finds himself involved in the case of his life. The defendant, David Hanson, was Mick's close friend in law school, and the victim, a TV news reporter, had reached out to Mick for legal help only hours before her death.Mick's played both sides of Philadelphia's courtrooms. As a top-shelf defense attorney and former prosecutor, he knows all the tricks of the trade. And he'll need every one of them to win.But as the trial progresses, he's disturbed by developments that confirm his deepest fears. This trial, one that already hits too close to home, may jeopardize his firm, his family--everything. Now Mick's only way out is to mastermind the most brilliant defense he's ever spun, one that will cross every legal and moral boundary.
demonstrations.review: I really enjoyed this book, a very twisty ending.  The author did a good job of fleshing out the characters.  The main character is an attorney who decides to represent an old law school friend in a murder and faces a lot of moral dilemmas throughout.  Just when I thought I had it figured out-I didn't.

demonstrations.item_text:
Lie After Lie: The True Story of A Master of Deception, Betrayal, and Murder
Kindle Edition

A seemingly perfect world held an even more unlikely killer... Julie Keown had a great job, financial security, and a perfect husband who was attending Harvard Business School. But after Julie suddenly died, and doctors discovered she's been poisoned with the main ingredient in antifreeze, her parents began to suspect that her husband, James, was not so perfect. This blow-by-blow account shows how investigators and state police unraveled James Keown's chilling web of deceit.
demonstrations.review: I had seen a special about the case and wanted to know more.  I wasn't disappointed except there wasn't much information about how James Keown grew up beyond his father was a well-known state lobbyist.  There is mention that he has older siblings he's not close to and did not attend his wife's funeral or his trial.  This speaks volumes and might have given a lot of insight into how he developed into the monster he became.  It seems to me even if those family members didn't want to speak out, there is usually plenty of other people who would have.

demonstrations.item_text:
The Flight Attendant: A Novel
Kindle Edition

NEW YORK TIMES BESTSELLER • A powerful thriller about the ways an entire life can change in one night: A flight attendant wakes up in the wrong hotel, in the wrong bed, with a dead man—and no idea what happened. • Don't miss the acclaimed HBO Max series! Cassandra Bowden is no stranger to hungover mornings. She's a binge drinker, her job with the airline making it easy to find adventure, and the occasional blackouts seem to be inevitable. She lives with them, and the accompanying self-loathing. When she awakes in a Dubai hotel room, she tries to piece the previous night back together, counting the minutes until she has to catch her crew shuttle to the airport. She quietly slides out of bed, careful not to aggravate her already pounding head, and looks at the man she spent the night with. She sees his dark hair. His utter stillness. And blood, a slick, still wet pool on the crisp white sheets. Afraid to call the police—she's a single woman alone in a hotel room far from home—Cassie begins to lie. She lies as she joins the other flight attendants and pilots in the van. She lies on the way to Paris as she works the first class cabin. She lies to the FBI agents in New York who meet her at the gate. Soon it's too late to come clean-or face the truth about what really happened back in Dubai. Could she have killed him? If not, who did?  Set amid the captivating world of those whose lives unfold at forty thousand feet, The Flight Attendant unveils a spellbinding story of memory, of the giddy pleasures of alcohol and the devastating consequences of addiction, and of murder far from home. Look for Chris Bohjalian's new novel, The Lioness !
demonstrations.review: As another review said, it drags on and on, then rushed at the end.  Very implausible ending and a little out of left field.  I only finished reading it because my sister highly recommended and we have similar tastes in books.  But she did tell me after she felt about the same with the ending.

demonstrations.item_text:
Second Honeymoon
Kindle Edition

In James Patterson's dazzling thriller, two secret agents hunt down a serial killer targeting honeymoon couples in Rome. A newlywed couple steps into the sauna in their deluxe honeymoon suite-and never steps out again. When another couple is killed while boarding their honeymoon flight to Rome, it becomes clear that someone is targeting honeymooners, and it's anyone's guess which happy couple is next on the list. FBI Agent John O'Hara is deep into solving the case, while Special Agent Sarah Brubaker is hunting another ingenious serial killer, whose victims all have one chilling thing in common.As wedding hysteria rises to a frightening new level, John and Sarah work ever more closely together in a frantic attempt to decipher the logic behind two rampages. From "The Man Who Can't Miss," Second Honeymoon is the most mesmerizing, most exciting, and most surprising thriller ever ( Time ).
demonstrations.review: Loved Honeymoon and now the follow-up Second Honeymoon.  Main characters are very likable and funny.  You can still read this book without reading the first one but I think it helps to know the backstory.

demonstrations.item_text:
Pat the Husband: A Parody
Spiral-bound – October 7, 2008

Paul snores. Paul snores so loudly, Judy cannot sleep. Paul tells Judy he does not snore. Paul is in denial. Judy has not had a good night’s sleep in years. Can you help Judy get a good night’s sleep? Dorothy Kunhardt’s Pat the Bunny is a timeless children’s classic, inspiring numerous spin-offs for both kids and adults—but none as wickedly amusing as this clever, hilarious, interactive book! Every wife, girlfriend, and woman who hopes to be one will treasure it and have endless fun playing with the lift-the-flap, touch-and-feel, pull tabs, and other highly designed elements. It slyly questions who wears the pants in the family, and lets women humor their men by removing the Velcro pants from the female figure and putting it on the male. Or, eager to have hubby say yes to your request? Then just use the tab to make his head nod! Since all men are really little boys at heart, what better way to celebrate (okay—roast) their peccadilloes than with a kids’ book format? Pat the Husband takes amusing aim at the oddities of guys everywhere, making it the perfect gift from girlfriend to girlfriend, as well as for bridal showers and anniversaries. Every wife will recognize the humor in the quirky characteristics played out about “husbands everywhere”—and find a reason every day to sneak a peek and pat!
demonstrations.review: I was buying a friend the Pat the Bunny for her little one and saw this book.  It is absolutely hysterical!  She and her husband loved it and she plans to bring it to a wedding shower.  Anyone in a relationship will get a kick out of it!

target.item_text:
1984
Mass Market Paperback – Unabridged, January 1, 1961

Written more than 70 years ago, 1984 was George Orwell’s chilling prophecy about the future. And while 1984 has come and gone, his dystopian vision of a government that will do anything to control the narrative is timelier than ever... • Nominated as one of America’s best-loved novels by PBS’s The Great American Read • “ The Party told you to reject the evidence of your eyes and ears. It was their final, most essential command. ”Winston Smith toes the Party line, rewriting history to satisfy the demands of the Ministry of Truth. With each lie he writes, Winston grows to hate the Party that seeks power for its own sake and persecutes those who dare to commit thoughtcrimes. But as he starts to think for himself, Winston can’t escape the fact that Big Brother is always watching...A startling and haunting novel, 1984 creates an imaginary world that is completely convincing from start to finish. No one can deny the novel’s hold on the imaginations of whole generations, or the power of its admonitions—a power that seems to grow, not lessen, with the passage of time.
target.review: I guess I can see why this is considered such a great book but I really could not get into it. The author is clearly talented, but there were parts of it that seemed to drone on for endless pages. It took me such a long time to get through it because I could only read small portions without getting bored. I don’t see what all of the hype is about. Sure there are some parallels to today’s society but it seems like a book for conspiracy nuts. It’s been on my list to read for a long time and I read all of it but overall I’m not impressed. There are tons better books to read.

demonstrations.item_text:
You Exist Too Much: A Novel
Paperback – June 8, 2021

A “provocative and seductive debut” of desire and doubleness that follows the life of a young Palestinian American woman caught between cultural, religious, and sexual identities as she endeavors to lead an authentic life ( O, The Oprah Magazine ). On a hot day in Bethlehem, a 12–year–old Palestinian–American girl is yelled at by a group of men outside the Church of the Nativity. She has exposed her legs in a biblical city, an act they deem forbidden, and their judgement will echo on through her adolescence. When our narrator finally admits to her mother that she is queer, her mother’s response only intensifies a sense of shame: “You exist too much,” she tells her daughter.Told in vignettes that flash between the U.S. and the Middle East—from New York to Jordan, Lebanon, and Palestine—Zaina Arafat’s debut novel traces her protagonist’s progress from blushing teen to sought–after DJ and aspiring writer. In Brooklyn, she moves into an apartment with her first serious girlfriend and tries to content herself with their comfortable relationship. But soon her longings, so closely hidden during her teenage years, explode out into reckless romantic encounters and obsessions with other people. Her desire to thwart her own destructive impulses will eventually lead her to The Ledge, an unconventional treatment center that identifies her affliction as “love addiction.” In this strange, enclosed society she will start to consider the unnerving similarities between her own internal traumas and divisions and those of the places that have formed her.Opening up the fantasies and desires of one young woman caught between cultural, religious, and sexual identities, You Exist Too Much is a captivating story charting two of our most intense longings—for love, and a place to call home.
demonstrations.review: I loved the idea of this book, but it was very poorly executed. I was expecting it to be much more in depth and meaningful with regard to culture and sexuality. But it reads as a moody, sexually confused, immature, teenager, who refuses to look at her own problems- when in reality it’s a 28 year old woman.

demonstrations.item_text:
American Gods: A Novel
Paperback – Illustrated, March 16, 2021

From #1 New York Times bestselling author Neil Gaiman, a contemporary masterpiece combing mythology, adventure, and illusion―one of ten classic Gaiman works repackaged with elegant original watercolor art by acclaimed artist Henry Sene Yee Released from prison, Shadow finds his world turned upside down. His wife has been killed; a stranger offers him a job and Shadow, with nothing to lose, accepts. But a storm is coming. Beneath the placid surface of everyday life, a war is being fought – and the prize is the very soul of America. An inspired combination of mythology, adventure, and illusion, American Gods is a dark and kaleidoscopic journey deep into myth and across an America at once eerily familiar and utterly alien. It is, quite simply, a contemporary masterpiece. “Piercingly observed, jaggedly poetic, ruthlessly cutting a path through graveyards of dead stars and dead money and dead feelings, this novel is the map back to dawn.”  — Steve Erickson “ American Gods manages to reinvent, and reassert, the enduring importance of fantastic literature itself in this late age of the world. Dark fun, and nourishing to the soul.” — Michael Chabon
demonstrations.review: This book started out very interesting but when I got halfway through I couldn’t force myself to finish it because it was so boring. The author is clearly a talented writer but this book has a lot of rambling sections that make absolutely no sense and overall the book is incredibly disorganized.

demonstrations.item_text:
American Dirt (Oprah's Book Club): A Novel
Hardcover – January 21, 2020

Jeanine Cummins's American Dirt , the #1 New York Times bestseller and Oprah Book Club pick that has sold over three million copies Lydia lives in Acapulco. She has a son, Luca, the love of her life, and a wonderful husband who is a journalist. But after her husband’s tell-all profile of the newest drug lord is published, none of their lives will ever be the same.Forced to flee, Lydia and Luca find themselves joining the countless people trying to reach the United States. demonstrations.review: It seems like people aren’t understanding the concept of fiction. Of course there’s going to be things that are a little far-fetched and it might be a little candy coated in some spots but overall this is an excellent book and I really enjoyed it. The author has clearly stated that she did her research when writing this book and anyone who expects it to be 100% accurate has unrealistic expectations. There’s misinformation out there everywhere whether it’s intentional or not. The author doesn’t claim that this is a personal, extremely accurate account of an immigrant’s experience. It’s a fictional story meant to provide some insight into what they go through. If someone had to have gone through something personally and be a complete expert on it in order to write a book there would be very few books written. I don’t see the people who write the DSM being screened for a mental health conditions or people who write history textbooks having their lineage researched.  People need to calm down and stop seeing and speaking for all people of one culture that they wouldn’t approve of this book. There’s a very small sliver of people who actually care about these things and those are the people giving the bad reviews.

The Girl with the Louding Voice: A Novel

AN INSTANT NEW YORK TIMES BESTSELLER A READ WITH JENNA TODAY SHOW BOOK CLUB PICK! “Brave, fresh . . . unforgettable.” — The New York Times Book Review “A celebration of girls who dare to dream.”—Imbolo Mbue, author of Behold the Dreamers (Oprah’s Book Club pick) Shortlisted for the Desmond Elliott Prize and recommended by The New York Times , Marie Claire , Vogue , Essence, PopSugar , Daily Mail, Electric Literature , Red, Stylist, Daily Kos , Library Journal , The Everygirl , and Read It Forward! demonstrations.review: I understand the point that this book was trying to make but it falls short. As other people have mentioned, the broken dialect is inconsistent. target.review: When I read the reviews of this book, it sounded like it was a unique novel that might provide a compelling story as well as some sound advice and/or techniques on how to succeed in marriage. demonstrations.item_text:
Team of Rivals: The Political Genius of Abraham Lincoln
Paperback – Illustrated, September 26, 2006

One of the most influential books of the past fifty years, Team of Rivals is Pulitzer Prize–winning author and esteemed presidential historian Doris Kearns Goodwin’s modern classic about the political genius of Abraham Lincoln, his unlikely presidency, and his cabinet of former political foes. Winner of the prestigious Lincoln Prize and the inspiration for the Oscar Award winning–film Lincoln , starring Daniel Day-Lewis, directed by Steven Spielberg, and written by Tony Kushner. On May 18, 1860, William H. Seward, Salmon P. Chase, Edward Bates, and Abraham Lincoln waited in their hometowns for the results from the Republican National Convention in Chicago. When Lincoln emerged as the victor, his rivals were dismayed and angry.  Throughout the turbulent 1850s, each had energetically sought the presidency as the conflict over slavery was leading inexorably to secession and civil war. That Lincoln succeeded, Goodwin demonstrates, was the result of a character that had been forged by experiences that raised him above his more privileged and accomplished rivals. He won because he possessed an extraordinary ability to put himself in the place of other men, to experience what they were feeling, to understand their motives and desires.  It was this capacity that enabled Lincoln as president to bring his disgruntled opponents together, create the most unusual cabinet in history, and marshal their talents to the task of preserving the Union and winning the war.  We view the long, horrifying struggle from the vantage of the White House as Lincoln copes with incompetent generals, hostile congressmen, and his raucous cabinet. He overcomes these obstacles by winning the respect of his former competitors, and in the case of Seward, finds a loyal and crucial friend to see him through.  This brilliant multiple biography is centered on Lincoln's mastery of men and how it shaped the most significant presidency in the nation's history.
demonstrations.review: It is easy to understand why this book was widely read and adapted into a film. It reads more like a novel and the characters are such a fascinating bunch. I don't use an electronic reader so my only issue was the physical weight of the book!

demonstrations.item_text:
Gilded Girls: Women Entertainers of the Old West
Paperback – June 1, 2003

The curtain rises and authors JoAnn Chartier and Chris Enss shine the spotlight on 14 entertaining women who sang, danced, acted in plays, performed equestrienne feats, and captured the hearts of the miners and homesteaders of the Frontier West. These "gilded girls" who performed in the mining boomtowns were literally showered with gold, but oftentimes their personal lives were marked by unhappiness. Still, their very presence on stage enchanted avid western audiences, and they were rewarded with flowery reviews and sensational editorials by local newspapers, as well as riches. Their every action was commented upon, but rarely did reporters know the whole story. Chartier and Enss now reveal what many people of the times never knew about these sometimes rowdy, sometimes refined female celebrities by providing a unique inside look at their lives via this collection of intriguing biographies.
demonstrations.review: This is a very well researched book and the subject matter is so entertaining and informative. Anyone who is interested in women, history and the old west would find it a terrific addition to their library.

demonstrations.item_text:
Wings of Freedom
Paperback – March 10, 2021

At the end of the Vietnam War, Pan American World Airways successfully evacuated 463 American and Vietnamese civilians on April 24, 1975, aboard a Boeing 747-the last plane out. At the time, Allen H. Topping was serving as the Pan Am Director of South Vietnam and Cambodia and was instrumental in the success of that last flight. Topping lived and worked in South Vietnam for two and a half years. In addition to its global network of scheduled services, Pan Am was also involved in many other rescue and humanitarian operations throughout the world. These operations and missions included the Berlin Airlift, rescue operations from Tehran, operational support for US forces in WW II, the Korean War, the Vietnam War and, most recently, the Gulf War. Prior to joining Pan Am Allan Topping worked for the Institute of International Education on and United Airlines in New York City. He joined Pan Am on June 2, 1969 as a sales representative, assigned to the San Francisco sales office. In November of 1972, Al became the Director of Vietnam and Cambodia, based in Saigon, South Vietnam. After managing operations at various stations overseas for almost eight years, he returned to the U.S. in 1982, Pan Am appointed him as Assistant to The Chairman Consumer Affairs. Topping continued to hold other management positions un���� l the company ceased operations on December 4, 1991. For the next 23 years he worked for The Miami-Dade School Board Administration, The Miami Herald and the Miccosukee Golf & Country Club in Miami, Florida. Now fully re���� red Topping is playing lots of golf in Ocala, Florida.
demonstrations.review: This is a well-written eye-witness account of a very heroic moment in the history of not just Pan Am but the United States as well. Al Topping deserves some kind of official recognition and acknowledgement from the U.S. Government for the role he played in organizing and executing the evacuation of Saigon. Right now we are facing a similar situation in Afghanistan. I hope there will be people like Al Topping helping to rescue those who have helped the U.S. effort in Afghanistan. It’s a fast read and an important one as well.

target.item_text:
His Christmas Angel (Heartsong Presents #509)
Mass Market Paperback – September 21, 2002

Matchmakers come in all different forms. Phillip McLean has been entrusted with the care of a family heirloom: a Chirstmas tree-topping angel ornament made by his grandmother long berfore he was born. When disaster strikes-the poor angel is stained by coffee-Phillip calls upon Grace, his best friend's girlfriend, to help fix it before Granny finds out. But that's not the end of it. Every time Phillip turns around, it seems, something else is happening to the angel. This ornament that was supposed to be a blessing has become a curse-except that it keeps sending him to Grace.... Meanwhile, Grace's emotiions are surging. She's liked Phillip for years, and now, seeing him so often, she's completely infatuated with him. Every time the angel comes back for repair, she gets a feeling like she's never had before. As Grace mends the crocheted angel, will her heart and Phillip's be knitted together?
target.review:
Phillip just got home with the prized family Christmas angel--the one his granny made decades ago, the one that has graced their trees every Christmas morning that he can remember--and now it's his. Phillip can't fully explain to his roommate, Neil, why the angel means so much to him, but it does. Within minutes, however, the priceless heirloom gets stained with coffee. Neil suggests his girlfriend, Grace--she's great at crafts and stuff; Phillip reluctantly calls her. And so begins an excruciating run of experiences where the antique crocheted angel encounters some catastrophe, Phillip runs to Grace for help, and Grace manages to fix the problem.
Meanwhile, Grace notices Phil for the first time. I mean, she's seen him occasionally at church but she's never spent actual time with him. Now, she's with him more than she's with Neil. She's happy to help out her boyfriend's best friend, but is there more happening than just repairing an angel?
Phillip's confusion over Grace and Neil's relationship multiplies when he starts feeling romantic affection for her; he tells himself it's wrong, that he should distance himself, but his heart won't listen. Could it be possible that God is trying to show him something about true love?

My Take:
I've never been fond of the 'friend falls for best friend's guy/girl' trope. Therefore, I wasn't sure how I felt about it here. Sure, Phillip and Grace don't intend to like each other romantically, and they both take steps to ensure proper boundaries. But eventually, Phillip questions Neil outright about his intentions toward Grace--is Neil thinking marriage someday (they've been dating for a year)? Neil is content with things as they are: he & Grace date exclusively, he watches hockey, she goes out with her girl friends, they do separate church ministries; why change anything? Grace is also led to introspection: her relationship with Neil is safe; he makes no demands on her time, her affection, anything; he's nice, reliable, hardworking; a man she could marry. After seeing the damage within her family by controlling husbands, Grace must guard her heart and be sure the man she marries will nurture and encourage her, not belittle and abuse.
While I could commend Grace for her selfless attention to Phillip's angel, it did seem odd that they sat in her living room with coffee, talking, when the work was done. Watching Grace and Phillip separately become attracted to each other and begin thinking about the other, etc., was a bit odd for me. I mean, I knew they were going to get together, that they were better matched than Neil and Grace, but the way it happened--I don't know. I guess Phillip was the catalyst for Neil and Grace to see that their relationship was "stagnant."
The angel. I don't crochet but I'm amazed at the intricate creations some people produce. Phillip's appreciation for Granny's talent rose with each mishap; it was cute seeing him participate in stringing tiny beads or dunking the angel in the sink. But I must say: after the 5th disaster, I quit counting. It seemed quite unrealistic that all these bad things kept happening to the angel--often within minutes of returning home with it fixed. It was exhausting, and I'm glad that after the first detailed repair, we got an abbreviated version. And what was the point of the whole gender debate? Grace called the angel a "she" while Phillip believed angels were portrayed as men in the Bible. They compromise and name the angel "Dale." Why didn't Grace look this up in her Bible? Was the discussion supposed to be cute? As for the angel itself, I couldn't picture it well in my mind, so kept referring to the book cover.

Toward the end of the story, after Phillip has confronted Neil about not spending enough time with Grace and has Neil considered marriage, Phillip gets aggravated and blurts out, "But I'm tired of playing second fiddle, Neil." Neil and Grace mutually realize they should have a serious talk. But before they can, Grace and Phillip must fix the angel at Grace's apartment.

"Do you love him?"
[There are paragraphs of Grace's thoughts.]
Phil stepped closer, until they stood toe-to-toe. "Well?"
"I-I don't know," she stammered.
Phil's voice dropped to a low rumble. "Then know this."
Before she realized what he was going to do, Phil . . . kissed her like she'd never been kissed before. With power and strength and confidence, and like he meant everything a kiss implied when holding her so close to his heart.

If you can endure 170 pages of an ill-fated angel (which is miraculously no worse for wear in the end), you'll get a lackluster proposal from Phillip and the promise of a happily ever after--on Christmas morning.

The Writing:
I like Gail Sattler's stories. This one doesn't have anything morally offensive and is very Christian. Written in 2002, phones still have cords and computers are still novel. There were moments of humor and sweetness. But reading "muttered" and "mumbled" a million times nearly drove me crazy! Whether the author, editor, or someone in between, it was like they substituted the word "said" with those 2 verbs. Did they not have a thesaurus? I don't remember any typos, but I was distracted by the mutters and mumblings, and the poor disaster-prone angel.

Overall:
It was mediocre. You could skip this book and be fine. But reading it won't hurt you. At ages 27 and 25, Phillip McLean and Grace Kramer can identify with being single, with following God's will, and with not knowing their own heart at times. Fortunately for them, God knew, and He used a handcrafted ornament to get them together. Phillip, Neil, and Grace are virtuous people, and their different personalities are highlighted. Love is beautiful but it also takes work and time. This book promotes Christian values during the season of Christmas.

demonstrations.item_text:
Michigan Brides (Romancing America)
Paperback – December 1, 2010

Relive Michigan’s industrial boom alongside three women who must change their way of viewing the world before they can realize love. Felicity does a very noble deed only to lead her to a romance that would be banned by her wealthy society. Annabelle’s interest in a potato picker is barred by the stigma society has placed on his ruined family. demonstrations.review:
"MICHIGAN BRIDES"
Amber Stockton
Romancing America series (2010)

“Copper and Candles”
1875, Detroit
Socialite Felicity Chambers feels fulfilled doing her charity work, so when a pregnant widow in a poor area of the city needs help, Felicity steps in. Literally. She goes to work in the candle factory, giving her wages to the widow. Felicity hasn’t quite thought through the ins and outs of leading a double life, but being independent and associating with girls her age minus the constraints of society is a refreshing change. Brandt Lawson, heir of the candle factory and copper refinery, is working incognito--per his father’s command--in order to learn all aspects of the business, before he assumes management. Brandt and Felicity share merging paths to work, so they walk together and form a friendship. Each assumes the other is beneath their wealthy status, and wishes society looked at a person’s heart and not their bank account or family connections. When both sets of parents conspire to pair Felicity and Brandt together, will the ruse that seemed innocent now destroy the relationship they value? Can they forgive each other for their deceit?
--I thought this was an okay story. The writing was solid and engaging. The main characters were fairly deep, although at times I wondered why they were angry or nervous. Brandt & Felicity are both rich, pretending to be poor, working in neighboring factories, feeling blessed and torn because they assume the other is in a lower social class. The confrontation seemed overly dramatic to me. Some loose ends: what did their co-workers/new friends think about them once they learned who they really were? How did the widow return to work in like a month, with a newborn plus 5 kids at home? Why was Felicity at the factory when the fire occurred?
We really don’t learn much about the actual work done in either factory. Physical appearance was adequate; details were reserved more for emotions. And as a rule, I’m not a fan of proposing marriage during grief or injury, although I realize some plots hinge on that. Overall, I thought this was a nice chaste story with sparse elements of faith, a lighthearted read, low on the history lesson side of things.

“Hearts and Harvest”
1894, Detroit
The eldest child of Felicity & Brandt has a heart of compassion and grace, and what greater way for Annabelle to show God’s love than to minister to the financially devastated? When her mission of kindness is received with skepticism and scorn, Annabelle trudges on, meeting two brothers who instantly attract her: 8-year-old Jacob and handsome but wary-eyed William Berringer. Annabelle goes out of her way to not only befriend but also bolster the faith of the brothers who now farm a plot her father donated. Just because her family wasn’t hit hard with the financial crisis doesn’t mean they were immune; however, Annabelle’s desire to aid the less fortunate stems from following God’s commands and her considerate nature. William used to be in Annabelle’s social position; now he’s wearing ill-fitting hand-out clothing and sweating in the dirt all day. His dreams are gone, his old life is gone, and even his beliefs about God are gone. Why can’t Annabelle just leave him alone? If God really did care and really was powerful, then why did He let this happen to them? They were a good family, making an honest living; why would He treat them so spitefully? In this unlikely soil of hurt, loss, and uncertainty, can faith be restored? And, can new love grow?
--I tried. But if a story can’t keep my attention after 5 chapters . . . And it’s not like you don’t know how it will end: Annabelle’s steady urgings will reignite William’s faith and he’ll again trust God, and the couple will become engaged/married. Happy ending. The pace was slow, William was surly (although with good reason), and there was a large cast tossed together--I didn’t know if I should try to remember these names for later, if these people had further bearing on the story. The financial collapse is explained at the very beginning, but I still didn’t know what happened; not being an industrial history buff, I knew nothing about Michigan having money troubles, or why, or what was done about it. Without understanding the money problem, the whole foundation for the story fell flat for me. I pushed onward through 1/3 of the story, then decided I had more interesting things I could read. That was the biggest issue: it didn’t keep my attention.

“Patterns and Progress”
(No date was readily given; sometime after 1912)
Now grown, Jacob Berringer is excited to pursue automobiles and other advances in industry. He thrills with each new invention. However, all Shannon sees is danger. She’s as against progress as Jacob is for it; how could a relationship develop between people with such opposing views?
--I didn’t read this story, just scanned some pages.

Well, having only read 1 of the 3 stories, I can’t really recommend or not recommend this book. I’ve read other novellas by this author--shorter stories--so maybe that suits me better. As far as learning about Michigan, I didn’t. Anyway, if you like this author or enjoy the Romancing America series, here’s one from 2010. (Also, often Barbour uses these older stories in newer collections, so keep that in mind.)

demonstrations.item_text:
Christmas Next Door: 4 Stories of Love Found Close to Home
Paperback – September 1, 2019

Visit an Old West Texas town where a mysterious benefactor leaves gifts each Christmas, but also where four pairs of neighbors battle over hearsay, secrets, and mysteries.   THE MARSHAL NEXT DOOR by Vickie McDonough (1885) The marshal’s deputy claims he’s seen the marshal’s young sisters snooping around businesses where there have been recent thefts. Marshal Yates can’t believe his sisters might be the thieves and seeks out a woman to mentor the impetuous teenagers. But when evidence is found against his sisters, will he have to arrest them at Christmastime?   THE SPINSTERS NEXT DOOR by Susan Page Davis (1886) Rachel Tanner’s family harbors secrets that may lead her and her aunts to financial ruin. When Stephen Worth rents a house on the Tanner property, he gets to close to family business, insisting Rachel open a locked box her dead father guarded closely. Can the schoolmaster persuade Rachel to defy her aunts and open the box—or will she remain alone with a tangle of unanswered questions?   THE OUTLAW NEXT DOOR by Vickie McDonough (1887) Dane McDermott, a reformed outlaw born into a gang of thieves, has buried his past deep. As respectable business owner Dane has finally met the woman of his dreams. But when his father shows up, will it ruin his chances for love with the preacher’s daughter?   THE GUNSLINGER NEXT DOOR by Susan Page Davis (1888) Alice Singer’s new neighbor has her worried. He’s a retired gunslinger with delusions that he is Ben Franklin and needs a printing press to produce his almanac. Enlisting the postmaster’s help, Alice seeks to understand her odd neighbor, his many packages, and mysterious visitors. Is he really just a harmless old fellow?
demonstrations.review:
The same Texas town, four consecutive Novembers, years 1885-88.

Justin & Marta--He's a protective brother and a stalwart marshal; she's the practical and kindhearted younger sister of his deputy. When he surprises her by asking for help with his teenage twin sisters, Marta is intimidated and thrilled. By teaching the girls how to cook and sew better, she interacts with Justin more and realizes the infatuation she's carried for 3 years may be something deeper. A series of thefts troubles Justin, but when evidence condemns his sister, he's overwhelmed. Marta prays and encourages him. Eventually the thief is caught--the bitter deputy (Marta's brother). Justin proposes on Christmas Eve.
**Right off I was swamped by a host of names. A large cast makes it feel like a real town, yes, but can be hard to keep everyone straight--even the twins' names threw me at times (Ella & Emma). I liked Justin's character, how conscientious and intuitive he was, and I liked seeing a lot of the story from his viewpoint. I didn't know Marta as well; she was a nice person, if a bit too perfect. There were mundane moments that lasted for pages, but most were meaningful for relationship development or plot details. This story had the most 'Christmas' in it--buying gifts, planning a meal, the burglary wrap-up happening on Christmas Eve. Overall, this was my favorite one.

Stephen & Rachel--He's the schoolmaster, helpful and good-natured; she's the heir and caretaker of her father's estate and aunts' welfare. Rachel defers to her aunts, feeling unworthy in some ways to assert herself due to a past mistake. Stephen was told Rachel was widowed, and when he rents their little house next door, he enjoys tea with the three ladies, getting to know all of them better--realizing he wants to court Rachel. But she stuns him by announcing she isn't a widow. Stephen (and the reader) has to wait a while before hearing the whole story: Rachel married at age 16 against her dad's wishes, her new husband was angry and abusive, and eventually left without a word; that was 12 years ago. On the night of the school's Christmas program, a mysterious locked box is stolen from Rachel's home. Stephen tackles the thief, recovers the box, and the foursome finally opens it. Besides money, they discover Rachel's husband was in prison and died 5 years prior. After the shock of this news abates, Rachel is free to accept Stephen's attentions.
**This was slow-going for me. Tedious accounts of where furniture was, the food they ate, etc., just made me want to skim ahead. I appreciated Rachel's loyalty to her father and aunts, but she didn't trust her own judgment because she had eloped as a teen--she thought she hadn't matured any since then, which saddened me. My biggest problem with this story was that Rachel allowed herself to fall for Stephen even though she was married (albeit in reality she was widowed, but she didn't know that); and when Stephen finds out she's married, he continues to see her and expresses his wish for a future. It just seemed like, especially in 1886, the honorable thing to do would've been to squelch any friendship that could lead to scandal/immorality, and I expected both these characters to guard their reputations (and hearts) more closely. The whole plot just muddied integrity.

Dane & Regina--He's got a past he wishes he could forget; she's the only child of the town pastor. There's more talk of the Christmas baskets (they are a ministry in each story) since Regina's mother organizes them every year. Not much beyond day-to-day happenings, until Dane's past pays a visit--a former gang member. When Dane's house goes ablaze, he rescues Regina and finally faces facts: he loves her but can't keep concealing his past. He explains everything to the marshal and the pastor, finding acceptance in their compassion. A shoot-out, a courtship, and the outlaw's son marries the preacher's daughter.
**Again, some drawn-out details tried to bore me, but I pushed through. We see how Regina and her parents struggle to show patience to an outspoken, even rude, aunt. I liked Dane, but Regina was pretty much a robot--not a stereotype pastors' kids would appreciate. And the ending with the outlaws, the day after the fire--a bit overdone for me. Christmas is shown in retrospect.

John & Alice--He's the helpful postmaster; she's a friendly, responsible daughter whose new neighbor causes her anxiety. The elderly former gunslinger thinks he's Ben Franklin, and John and Alice worry about him. When things escalate, Alice is held prisoner by counterfeiters while John and the marshal rescue her. John pronounces his desire to marry her, and her dad approves.
**This story was fraught with daily chores, meals, chit-chat, nice conversations like, 'How are you today?'/'I am well, thank you. How are you?' Yeah, I know people are polite and everything, but it got in the way of the story's movement. I realized the gunslinger was a counterfeiter before Alice did, which must mean she's not as suspicious as me! We do find out the identity of the mystery poultry donor (for the Christmas baskets). This is the only story of the 4 that the main characters didn't live next door. There was a little humor and a couple sweet moments, but not enough.

Overall, if you're looking for a Christmas book that occurs near the holiday, mentions greenery, gifts, and charity, and has romance, then you'll be fine with this. When I think of a Christmas book, I expect Christmas to be a major theme, a contributor to the story. Finding love in your own hometown is always a great touch, and even without snow, these novellas accomplish that. Add solid yet subtle faith and clean romances, and this light-to-medium read is good for any time of the year.

demonstrations.item_text:
Under His Wings - Hymns of Comfort & Hope: Piano Solo
Paperback – June 1, 2011

(Lillenas Publications). This collection is devotional in nature with beloved hymns that are particularly well-suited for funerals, memorial services and life celebrations. However, they certainly are not limited to those settings. They are filled with themes of hope, promise and comfort making them also good considerations for prayer, prelude, communion and other similar roles in the weekly worship service. Sample hymns in this collection include "Amazing Grace," "It Is Well with My Soul," "Near to the Heart of God," and "What a Friend We Have in Jesus," to name a few.
demonstrations.review: Let me say, perspective.  While I borrowed this book and found it below my playing level, I did like several things. The intros on "Does Jesus Care?" and "Near to the Heart of God" are pretty, and I thought "It Is Well with My Soul" had potential (used some different chords from the normal hymn). I also liked pairing "What a Friend" with "In the Garden" (medleys are maybe's for me). However, most of the songs just start and stop abruptly, with no intro or climax, so I was left with longing. Some of the chording was fresh but repetitious. But, my mom--for whom I bought the book--was excited because this collection was doable for her; she doesn't play arranged hymns because they're too hard, so this is a nice workable challenge. Overall, "moderate" is probably a good description.

demonstrations.item_text:
Australia: Search for Tomorrow/Search for Yesterday/Search for Today/Search for the Star (Inspirational Romance Collection)
Paperback – January 1, 2000

Go down under with a contemporary collection of three complete novels and one novella.
demonstrations.review:
I got this book from a library, not remembering if I'd read the author's work before. While there were parts of her style I found compelling (like some cute Australian phrasing), it wasn't enough to compensate for my time. I couldn't picture myself in Australia. The unclear spiritual beliefs were confusing. The characters, plagued by simple miscommunications, nearly made life-changing decisions. These are the areas that stood out most as problems for me. And I only read the first two stories.

"Search for Tomorrow" -- I did appreciate the lack of graphic details regarding the car wreck. Jim is exceedingly patient and understanding with Gail; her personality rang authentic and appealing. I didn't like how 2 unmarried people reside in the same house (with Jim's mom and teenage brother) and fall in love, even briefly kiss. I have no idea what they believed spiritually--there was 'Sister' Jean Drew who was 'converted' and followed Jesus, and Jim's family is loving, reads the Bible, prays; but vague.
"Search for Yesterday" -- I didn't really know Hilda, and Rance bewildered me. The author was tackling heavy issues: secret adoption, drugs, pre-marital sex, physical abuse, religious condemnation. Again, we have 2 single people (obviously attracted to each other prior) staying in the same house--with a traumatized son and daytime housekeeper. There were some passionate moderately-detailed kisses. The mystery premise of the book gets little attention, and wraps up too nicely.

Maybe my expectations were excessive. After all, we have chaste couples who grow as individuals; 'contemporary' plots that aren't outdated some 25+ years later; folks who rely on faith and value integrity. Any author who addresses forgiving a supposed 'killer,' dealing with keen emotional trauma, and handling neglect and abuse, deserves credit. And I'm glad she linked God to all these situations. Perhaps she was being purposely fuzzy to avoid being preachy. Maybe I should've read the other 2 stories. Unfortunately, I personally feel disappointed here, except by assuring you that authors who constantly overuse adverbs can indeed certainly get published.

demonstrations.item_text:
Love Finds You In Bethlehem New Hampshire
Hardcover – January 1, 2009

Hardback
demonstrations.review:
Can I say I loved the cover! But other than that, this book fell flat for me.

When I read the glowing reviews, I expected a slow, simple, charming story--something lighthearted but worthwhile. Sadly, I regret spending 2 days of reading time on this. So I'll detail some points that I wish I had known beforehand.

I found Tom & Sara to be fickle and spiritually immature.

The book is 295 pages; they don't actually meet till pg. 92. At first Sara lives with Tom & his sister. Later she'll be at a guesthouse, then a kind family's home. All those changes are abrupt.

Sara is called determined, but came off conflicted to me. The way she sways from wanting Tom to love her, to wondering if she should leave, to everything in between, with no rhyme or reason--it was irritating. (Albeit she is 18. To Tom's 30. Though I'm not sure they were that far apart mentally.)

As for depicting Tom as a devout Christian, I don't recall him once reading a Bible (although several times he quotes parts of verses), and church is a mere mention. While he frequently prays, where does he expect to find answers if not in the Bible where God 'speaks' to us? And his friendship with beautiful Annabelle--? I sympathize that he wanted to keep his options open since he didn't know what he should do, but never once did he bring up spiritual matters with her. And he considered marriage! Would a man that earnest in his walk with God forget to ask his potential bride if she shared his faith? These are just a few things that made him inconsistent to what everyone testified. On the upside, I learned about painting landscapes, and did see Tom's creative heart.

All the impulsive 'disappearances' seemed only to serve as filler. It could've been done in a comical way, a heartwarming way, but instead it was like, 'Sara ran out the door. Tom didn't go after her. He didn't know if he wanted to.' They were constantly having misunderstandings--often because of circumstantial issues--but after a while it grew tiresome. I sincerely doubt they could've fallen in love given their lack of interaction.

We 'hear' much about Sara's life of homelessness but 'see' little. In fact, when Tom rushes to NYC looking for her, I felt like then I glimpsed the crowded streets, the contrasting mix of poor and rich folks, the loneliness. To me, that was one of the most interesting and meaningful portions of the whole story, and the author did well bringing us along with Tom.

The strongest relationship was Tom and his childhood friend, Lawrence. They were candid, supportive, and knew each other well. Despite Lawrence making no profession of salvation, his heart was softening.

Sooo, that was a lot to say this: I was frustrated and disappointed. The plot was slow, but Sara & Tom's relationship was not simple--due to their inability to communicate, understand their own feelings, know what true love was. I wasn't charmed. But the kisses were chaste, the conduct proper (it was 1890, a Gilded Age tourist town), the community of Bethlehem was realistic, and the descriptions of the mountains/scenery were well done. But I guess, like Tom, I was expecting something different than I found in this story.

target.item_text:
Cracking Health Costs
Hardcover – June 21, 2013

Cracking Health Costs reveals the best ways for companies and small businesses to fight back, right now, against rising health care costs. This book proposes multiple, practical steps that you can take to control costs and increase the effectiveness of the health benefit. The book is all about rolling back health care costs to save companies and employees money. Working hand-in-hand with their employees, businesses need to ensure that, whenever feasible, employees with the most expensive diagnoses get optimal treatment at hospitals not practicing “volume-driven” medicine for higher profits. Less than 10% of employees incur 80% of costs. About 20% of patients have been completely misdiagnosed, while many others are simply the victims of surgeons who are either practicing bad medicine or overtreating for profit. For example, some companies, such as Walmart and Lowe’s, are turning to the “Centers of Excellence” approach author Tom Emerick helped to pioneer while running benefits for Walmart. By determining which hospitals are adopting the highest standards of care, benefits managers can reduce the number of unnecessary high-cost surgeries and improve employees’ overall health. The solution-based approach offered by the book is unique, because it can be implemented by businesses today.
target.review:
To those who work in healthcare population management, Al Lewis has long been known as an avid self-promoter who thinks very highly of himself and his theories. But at least Al tends to show a sense of humor when he summarily dismisses the work of others and, in some cases, insults their intelligence.

Tom Emerick, on the other hand, lacks the sense of humor entirely.

If you are an executive who would like to get rid of employees who have health issues in their family and discourage everyone from using their health insurance, you'll probably love this book.

On the other hand, the concept of centers of excellence in health care that was first developed in the 1960's and implemented by Medicare in the 1990's has some validity in terms of managing healthcare costs. Unfortunately, the reader may come away with the impression that Mr. Emerick was somehow instrumental in the development and implementation of this widely accepted concept.

All in all, a short and somewhat interesting read with an absolutely tiresome number of self-promoting references to the authors.

demonstrations.review:
As always, while going about his everyday life as a handsome, fearsome and wealthy globe-trotting marine explorer, Dirk Pitt manages to accidently become involved in fantastically dangerous and adventureous situations that he manages to survive and end up a hero.

Unfortunately, it seems like these situations are starting to stray across the line from amusingly unbelievable to ridiculously unbelievable.

In the serial fiction world of adventure hero novels, that's a line you really don't want to cross. Instead of coming up with brilliant strategies and solutions that impress the reader, the hero ends up pulling dumb stunts and getting lucky.

demonstrations.review:

demonstrations.review: I listened to the audio version.  This book is the quintessential page turner, or whatever you call an audio book that keeps you up at night.  I personally have switched to audio books because the glow of my iPad somehow prevents me from falling asleep, even when I'm tired.  I'll skip the plot summary, since every other review seems to have that covered.  I'll try to list a few cons.  I listened to the unabridged version.  At points I thought the story dragged, but those moments were rare.  I'm sure if I had listened to the abridged version, I wouldn't have anything to complain about. But I didn't want to miss any details-yes I'm somewhat ambivalent.  Some would say Reacher is larger than life, like an 80's action flick protagonist.  I personally don't have a problem with that.  This is no Michael bay screenplay.  Childs writes with a certain cadence.  I'm not an English major and it's definitely not iambic pentameter, but it draws you in and makes your heart beat faster.  I cannot rank this novel again this other Reacher novels, but it's definitely 5 stars from me.

demonstrations.review:
A scan of a book published in 1906, so some of the information may not be correct. But for an amateur genealogist like me, it's a great starting point. There were several George Abbotts who came to Essex County, Massachusetts. This book follows the line of the one who died in Rowley, MA in 1647, to the seventh generation. It says "Volume I" in small print on the title page. There's no index of names. Most of it is very legible, but at least four of the pages (32-33 and 545-546) are barely readable, and only by someone who was willing to take the time to decipher the lines and scratches. The recto pages only of the TOC, List of Illustrations, and list of Abbreviations are cut off on the right hand edge so 2 or 3 letters are missing from all the words on those margins. The pedigree, which spans two pages, is badly truncated in the middle and on the right margin, so that several names are impossible to read. You can figure it out from the text, though I'm not sure the spouses' names and pertinent dates are in the text or not. It ends rather abruptly with Nathaniel Abbott (generation 6) and his children.

Volume 2 apparently covers the line of George Abbott of Andover, Massachusetts. I don't have that book. I don't know if it has the index for both volumes, or if there just isn't an index.

demonstrations.review:
Well, it's from 1839, innit? So not all of the information is up to date, and it's possible some of the details are no longer correct. That's always the risk with these older books. But it's still a great resource. Some towns get several pages, some towns get a paragraph. The old-fashioned font is hard on the eyes, and some pages are quite faced, but so far, everything has been perfectly readable. Organized by county in alphabetical order, then alpha by town within the county. Includes all 14 counties: Barnstable, Berkshire, Bristol, Dukes (just Martha's Vineyard: Chilmark, Edgartown, and Tisbury), Essex, Franklin, Hampden, Hampshire, Middlesex, Nantucket (just Nantucket Island and town), Norfolk, Plymouth, Suffolk, and Worcester. Two-page preface, followed by a table of contents listing every town and its page number, then a good index listing some founders' and settlers' names, the illustrations, and a good number of topics and events of interest. Where sources are quoted, the print is smaller, and in some cases there are quotes within quotes and that print is excruciatingly tiny, but readable.

If you'd like to know whether a town is included or not, please ask. There are way too many to list. Bear in mind that some towns may have changed counties since 1839.

target.review:

demonstrations.review:
This book is a great introduction to some of the basic concepts of physics. However, what was lacking was a thorough explanation where formulas are involved. A lot of the examples gave the correct formula to use and gave the answer but didn't actually work all the way through the formula from beginning to end. For someone well-versed in physics, this may be fine, but not for the average reader.

This is not an example out of the book but should help you understand what I'm talking about.

5x + 7 = 32
Answer = x = 5

That's fine if you know algebra and know how to find x, but the middle steps are missing.

All-in-all, a great read, funny and entertaining, but not for someone looking to actually learn physics.

demonstrations.review:
I'm only about 1/4 of the way through the book, but so far, I'm thoroughly enjoying it. Almost as much as I did reading it the first time, over a decade ago, in Richard Laymon's "Night in the Lonesome October".

The author had, without doubt, been a Laymon fan, and imitation must indeed be the sincerest form of flattery, as the storyline is almost identical to Laymon's book.

Both take place in October. Both have a main character who roams the streets at night looking for a "mystery girl". The mystery girl, in turn, is homeless and sleeps in people's homes when they away. Even Midnight's crazy, bicycle-riding drug dealer is reminiscent of Lonesome October's cackling bike hag. Even the use of the word "cackle" itself seems to have found its way into both books at similar places in the story.

Don't get me wrong, I'm loving "The Face of Midnight", but I can't help but believe that the author took a few too many elements from Laymon's book.
